# Better Prompting for Federal Work

<!-- vimeo: 1218358367 | track: English (auto-generated) -->

[▶ Watch on Vimeo](https://vimeo.com/1218358367)

<details>
<summary>자막: Better Prompting for Federal Work</summary>

When an AI response misses the mark, the first instinct is often, "Maybe the prompt needs work." Sometimes that is true. OpenAI's guidance offers a simple starting point. Outline the task, give helpful context, and describe the ideal output. For federal work, name the audience, attach current guidance, and ask for a one-page brief in plain language. Be specific, but keep it simple. If you are not sure what context the AI needs, ask it to pause and ask you clarifying questions before it begins. That can surface missing details or constraints before they affect the result. Treat prompting as a conversation. Review the first response, then refine the request with focused feedback. But prompting is not always the problem. Imagine asking an AI assistant to brief an agency leader on a new federal policy. Even a beautifully written prompt cannot help if the assistant does not have the current policy, cannot access the supporting guidance, or has no way to tell which source is authoritative. The same is true when a task requires access the AI has not been granted, involves records or sensitive information that must be handled appropriately, needs a decision only an accountable official can make, or lacks a clear review process. Before rewriting the prompt for the tenth time, ask four questions. Does the AI have the right information? Does it have the right tools, permissions, and approved information? Is the task appropriate for AI, and is there a clear way to evaluate the result? Better prompts matter, but reliable outcomes in government come from the whole system: clear instructions, authoritative context, approved tools, thoughtful evaluation, and human judgment where it counts. AI outputs are drafts, so apply your usual accuracy, legal, privacy, records management, and accessibility reviews. The goal is not to find magic words. It is to design a better way of working.
